items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: That quality of expression for me began with the Charles Lloyd Quartet. It actually began, we were, I remember during our first performance in Antibes France, this is Jack DeJohnette, Keith Jarrett, myself and Charles Lloyd.

ctx.x: Well I’m not sure what I mean and I’m glad you asked that. It seems that the music had a reason for being other than just we have, you know we got a recording date, different from perhaps when a bop musician would get a date and they would get six or seven tunes together, some that they had written and some standards, where the music that you were involved in in the 60s seemed to have another level to it, that there was an intent to affect people as they listened.

Yes. That quality of expression for me began with the Charles Lloyd Quartet. It actually began, we were, I remember during our first performance in Antibes France, this is Jack DeJohnette, Keith Jarrett, myself and Charles Lloyd. We followed, we were fortunate to follow Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald in Southern France right at the edge of the Mediterranean with maybe 3- 4,000 people seated outside sort of in an ampitheatrical set up there. We followed Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald with the…

would sometimes come from a place that I don’t even know about. When I was a young man of course there was the church and there was the community where you heard music that made you, that called your attention to persons or groups that were feeling something. So the Charles Lloyd group was one that prepared me for that Alice Coltrane recording, because that “Journey in Satchidananda” meant that she was going there to pray, to respect the gods of her choice, you know, so far as being her continued existence…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: so I suggested Cecil McBee, and then the Charles Lloyd Quartet was formed.

ctx.x: Chuck Mangione and his brother Gap?

Chuck Mangione! Chuck Mangione was playing trumpet. Frank Mitchell was playing tenor saxophone and Keith was playing piano on a song called "Buttercorn Lady.” Charles asked me about a pianist, and Charles had heard Keith in Boston and so we both said "Oh! Keith, let's get Keith!" Then Reggie didn't work out so I'd been playing with Cecil so I suggested Cecil McBee, and then the Charles Lloyd Quartet was formed. So I was still doing some freelancing around New York. I got a chance to play with McCoy and Joe…

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: mean playing with Jack and Keith were just all I was about.

ctx.x: No. I didn’t record with Miles Davis, but I had an episode with Miles Davis. Herbie Hancock called me — well what’s that, my first recording we discussed before, with Grachan Moncur featuring Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams. This is how I met Herbie and those guys. And so apparently I was rather impressive with my dynamic. Herbie called me and says, “Miles would like you to do a performance with him.” So I said, “Yeah, okay.” And by now, I mean that was like a couple of years later. By now I’m…

mean playing with Jack and Keith were just all I was about. But on 77th Street on the third floor of Miles’ brownstone we had gone through all the tunes, the music was like that — right? And no Miles Davis. Right? So at the conclusion of the rehearsal, the last tune in the Key of C there was Herbie and Wayne were at the piano discussing the voicing of a G something chord, a G 7 chord. And they couldn’t find it. All of a sudden burst through the door was Miles Davis. He went over to the piano and he said…
Well he was a boxer, wasn’t he?
